Elden Ring is an experience unlike anything I’ve played before. FromSoftware took the best elements of its previous Soulsborne games and seamlessly brought them together in a vast, interconnected open world. It feels like the culmination of everything the studio has learned and perfected over the past decade. The first impression of Limgrave is outstanding. The atmosphere is breathtaking, the landscapes are stunning, and the sheer sense of scale and mystery immediately draws you into the world. Every corner of the map holds something new to discover, whether it’s a hidden cave, an ancient ruin, or an unexpected boss encounter. The world constantly rewards curiosity and makes exploration feel genuinely exciting. You never quite know what awaits you beyond the next hill and that sense of discovery is what makes the experience so special.

The combat is equally outstanding. It feels smooth, challenging, and incredibly rewarding. The boss fights are another major highlight, offering a huge variety of enemies and memorable battles that constantly challenge you to adapt. The variety of weapons, spells, and abilities allows you to experiment with different builds and find your own approach to almost every encounter. What truly elevates Elden Ring, however, is how its systems work together. The items you discover can fundamentally change how you approach the game. This variety also gives Elden Ring exceptional replayability. A second playthrough can feel like a completely different adventure simply because you choose another build, discover areas you missed the first time or approach familiar encounters with a new perspective. The world is so densely packed with content that completing the main story is only one part of what the game has to offer. 

And then there is the Shadow of the Erdtree expansion, which is absolutely worth experiencing. It builds upon the strengths of the base game with new environments, challenging enemies, memorable boss encounters, and an impressive amount of additional content. The difficulty can be demanding, but that is part of what makes the experience so rewarding. Rather than feeling like an unnecessary addition, the expansion feels like a substantial continuation of the adventure and further demonstrates FromSoftware's ability to create compelling worlds filled with secrets and challenges.

What makes all of this especially meaningful to me is how rarely a game manages to leave such a lasting impression. The last time I felt this much joy and love for a game was around 15 years ago with Elder Scrolls Skyrim. Both games capture that feeling of stepping into a new world and wanting to explore every corner of it. For me, it is one of the most memorable gaming experiences in recent years and a genuine masterpiece of the open-world RPG genre. Everything Elden Ring has to offer makes it an incredible gaming experience. If you enjoy immersive worlds, rewarding combat, meaningful exploration, and the freedom to shape your own adventure, I cannot recommend Elden Ring highly enough. It’s been a long time since a game resonated with me this much. I genuinely wish I could experience it all over again for the first time. I highly recommend playing it!

Elden Ring is a good game, but it's so bogged down by its own weight that I don't think I've ever encountered a game that's overstayed its welcome to this degree. 

Prior to playing, I'd read the criticisms of reused content and open world recycling, but I genuinely didn't think it would be as bad as it actually is. You know that meme, where it's [Game] (picture of things clustered together) and [Open World Game] (picture of same things spaced apart)? I don't think that actually captures the dynamic of Elden Ring. That sentiment implies that an open-world game has bespoke, quality content with stretches of empty space between them. In reality, the situation is actually worse in Elden Ring. It's not that there's quality content separated by empty space -- it's actually mediocre content separated by empty space.

So, so, SO much of the content in Elden Ring simply isn't worth doing, at all. Your first Catacomb is worth doing for novelty, sure, but the fifth and tenth one certainly aren't. You will find the same exact enemy types and design principles in every single one -- by having experienced one Catacomb, you have experienced them all (and the first experience, frankly, isn't particularly memorable anyhow). Sadly, Catacombs are actually one of the more interesting POI types in Elden Ring, since they tend to have more involved  layouts and traps. Other POI types, like Caves, are abysmally boring, being indistinct, featureless tunnels, and some, like Ruins, barely qualify as content at all, being literally a staircase into a chest and nothing more. To add insult to injury, rewards are infrequently worth your time, often being a consumable material you have dozens of and a spirit ash no human in history has ever actually equipped to their hotbar. These two things, in tandem, mean that exploring POIs in Elden Ring have neither intrinsic nor extrinsic value -- you don't want to do them for their own sake, and you don't want to do them for the item rewards, either.

The result of this dynamic is that nothing in Elden Ring really feels new past the first area. In them, the majority of things to find are the same stale, bland POIs you've already experienced. Liurnia might as well be Blue Limgrave, Caelid be Red Limgrave, Altus Yellow Limgrave, and so on. While they might be "new" areas, they house the same tired content you've already experienced prior to entering them. In that way, the entire world collapses. Reuse is the name of the game: POIs, enemies, bosses, field enemies. I found myself actively skipping most field content past the 40-50 hour mark. Why make a 80-100 hour game, then, if much of it isn't worth playing? It calls into question the entire open-world format; it's structurally flawed, and Elden Ring is no exception. You have functionally experienced 80% of the gameplay loop by the time you have cleared the Weeping Peninsula.

What about the other 20%, then? Well, the other 20% is some of the best content in video gaming, ever. The legacy dungeons -- the actual quality, bespoke content one might hope to see in a video game -- are truly exceptional. Areas like Leyndell and Nokstella will simply astonish you with their atmosphere, layout, and exploration. These zones are exceptional, and the usual Soulslike successes -- weighty combat, tense experience loss mechanics -- shine as you make your way through these imaginative and exhilarating zones. They evoke fantastical wonder and white-knuckle adrenaline in equal measure.

Legacy dungeons are truly a joy to play through, but they beg the obvious question: why weren't these the whole game? Why did Fromsoft waste so much time on ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Cave #20-30 instead of just developing actually good content? Elden Ring feels open world for the sake of being open world -- the structure adds very little, if anything, to the game but takes so much. The opportunity cost of developing at scale is too steep to ameliorate, even for veteran developers with the resources and creative freedom to execute their vision somewhat faithfully. I understand that there's a sense of epicness that comes with a sheer size, but I don't think it was worth it for Elden Ring. The game would be twice as good if it were half the size, filled with content that's actually worth doing. I understand the desire to break away from the Dark Souls brand, but, in my opinion, nothing about the trade was worth it -- especially so since the best parts of the game (like interwoven dungeon layouts, expanded character movesets, and weapon art customizability) are just Dark Souls+.

Ultimately, I do recommend Elden Ring, but with the heavy caveat that it is the victim of its own ambition. The game is too big, too empty, too formulaic for its own good. I do understand why Elden Ring is beloved, and I do understand why it's such a seminal title in gaming. I'll also admit that I've never particularly cared for the open-world format. But I truly believe that, subjective opinions aside, it does more harm than good to Elden Ring. I've played for about 80 hours, enjoyed much of it, and am very near the end of the game, but I simply don't have the stamina to continue. Maybe I'll pick it up again in the future, but the friction is grinding.

There's enjoyment to be had, but be warned: you have a lot of chores to do between the fun.

Elden Ring – A master...piece of ♥♥♥♥

Elden Ring is a weird game. Beautiful graphics, fantastic combat, incredible world design, yet I spent much of my playthrough wondering whether I was having fun.
The world is full of memorable places, classic FromSoftware gameplay, and some genuinely fun enemies and bosses.
And then there's Torrent. The horse. The legend. The actual secret weapon. Forget legendary swords. Running past 90% of the nonsense is probably the most useful ability in the game.

Elden Ring has two gameplay modes: explore endlessly or git gud.

Exploration becomes exhausting. The world is enormous, yet regular enemies are barely a threat. You spend hours checking every cliff and cave, collecting hundreds of items you'll never use.
Another cookbook? Fantastic. Another crafting material? Just what I needed.
The game makes you explore every edge of the map because maybe something useful is hidden there. Spoiler: usually there isn't. Or it's not what you need.

Then there's the difficulty balance.

Without Mimic Tear, some bosses feel like beating a brick wall with a toothpick. With Mimic Tear, suddenly you're the brick wall. There's little middle ground between getting destroyed and watching your clone do half the work.
I love challenging combat, but I'd rather feel I won than found the unofficial easy-mode switch. 

And finally, the story.

Cryptic lore, depressing characters, dying worlds, NPCs speaking in riddles. Classic FromSoftware. But Elden Ring feels particularly bleak. I never felt like a hero.
The Chosen Undead in DS1 and Ashen One in DS3 weren't traditional heroes either. These games are about struggling through broken worlds. But Elden Ring gave me little reason to care about becoming Elden Lord.

The verdict?

Brilliant ideas, fantastic combat, breathtaking environments, memorable moments.
Also bloated, repetitive, frustrating, and obsessed with rewarding exploration with stuff nobody needs.
When it's good, it's brilliant. When it's bad, you're riding Torrent around another cliff looking for an item you'll never use.

A game I can admire more easily than I can love.

A 10,000-line review will not fit in one response. I can write it in numbered parts, keeping the review overwhelmingly positive and avoiding repetition.

Elden Ring: A Monumental Triumph of Open-World Design

Elden Ring is not merely a successful action role-playing game. It is a vast, mysterious, and deeply rewarding adventure that demonstrates what an open world can achieve when discovery matters more than checklists. FromSoftware takes the demanding combat, intricate environments, and cryptic storytelling associated with its earlier games and expands them across the Lands Between without sacrificing their identity.

The opening hours establish the game's confidence immediately. After a brief introduction, the player emerges into Limgrave and sees a landscape filled with ruins, forests, cliffs, castles, and distant landmarks. The game does not overwhelm the screen with icons or insist upon a rigid itinerary. Instead, it invites curiosity. A ruined church may contain a merchant. A forest might conceal an underground elevator. A distant tower could become the beginning of an adventure lasting several hours.

This approach makes exploration feel personal. Players are not simply clearing activities selected from a menu; they are constructing their own journeys. One person may travel directly toward Stormveil Castle, while another spends hours investigating caves, fighting optional bosses, gathering equipment, and discovering characters in unexpected locations. Both experiences feel valid because the world accommodates different priorities without losing its carefully designed structure.

The Lands Between is enormous, but its scale is supported by remarkable environmental variety. Limgrave's green plains create a welcoming yet melancholy beginning. Liurnia of the Lakes surrounds the player with mist, flooded ruins, and magical institutions. Caelid presents a diseased landscape whose crimson skies and grotesque creatures communicate danger before a single enemy attacks. Later territories continue to introduce distinctive architecture, weather, terrain, and atmosphere.

These regions are visually memorable because they do more than change the scenery. Each area produces a different emotional response. Limgrave encourages adventurous confidence. Caelid inspires dread. Leyndell creates awe through its immense golden architecture and layered streets. The Mountaintops of the Giants convey isolation through snow, wind, and tremendous empty spaces. The environments serve as storytelling devices, shaping the player's understanding of a fractured world.

Torrent, the player's spectral steed, makes this immense landscape pleasurable to traverse. Torrent moves quickly, can double-jump, and gives exploration a sense of freedom. The mount allows players to leap over obstacles, climb unconventional routes, and escape dangerous encounters. Mounted combat adds another dimension, particularly when fighting dragons or groups of enemies across open fields.

The absence of excessive guidance is one of the game's greatest strengths. Elden Ring trusts players to observe their surroundings. Statues can point toward hidden catacombs. Unusual rock formations may indicate concealed paths. A distant structure can become a navigational reference. Even the fragments required to reveal each portion of the map must be found in the world, turning cartography into part of the adventure.

The map itself is beautifully designed. Rather than functioning as a sterile interface, it resembles an illustrated artifact filled with geographical clues. Drawn ruins, mines, forests, and unusual formations encourage investigation. A careful player can often predict where something interesting might be located without the game explicitly identifying it. This preserves mystery while rewarding attention.

Combat remains the foundation of the experience. Every encounter asks the player to consider distance, timing, stamina, positioning, and enemy behaviour. Attacks have weight, shields provide meaningful protection, and dodges demand judgment. Victory rarely comes from pressing buttons thoughtlessly. Even ordinary opponents can punish carelessness, which makes successful encounters satisfying.

The game's difficulty is demanding, but it is unusually flexible. Players can improve their attributes, upgrade weapons, summon spirits, use cooperative multiplayer, exploit elemental weaknesses, or leave a difficult area and return later. These options do not trivialise the adventure. They create multiple ways to overcome its challenges and allow a broader range of players to find a workable strategy.

Build diversity is exceptional. A character can become a heavily armoured knight, a swift duelist, a destructive sorcerer, a faithful healer, an archer, or a warrior who combines several disciplines. The enormous selection of weapons, spells, shields, talismans, armour sets, and consumable items encourages experimentation. Discovering a new piece of equipment can inspire an entirely different style of play.

Weapons feel distinct rather than interchangeable. Colossal swords strike slowly but deliver tremendous impact. Spears control space and allow cautious attacks. Curved swords reward aggression and mobility. Bows offer ranged utility, while magical staffs and sacred seals open extensive spell systems. Even weapons within the same category may possess different attack patterns, scaling properties, or special abilities.

The Ashes of War system deepens this variety. These abilities can grant weapons dramatic techniques, from powerful leaps and spinning attacks to magical projectiles and defensive manoeuvres. Many Ashes of War also allow players to modify a weapon's affinity, helping it complement a chosen distribution of attributes. The system makes ordinary equipment adaptable and gives experimentation practical value.

Magic is particularly impressive. Sorceries and incantations are not limited to variations of basic projectiles. Players can summon spectral weapons, manipulate gravity, breathe like dragons, hurl lightning, conjure flames, cure ailments, strengthen allies, and unleash enormous beams of magical energy. The visual spectacle supports a system with genuine tactical breadth.

Spirit Ashes are another valuable addition. These summonable companions range from packs of wolves to powerful individual warriors. They can distract bosses, apply status effects, or contribute substantial damage. More importantly, they let players shape the rhythm of difficult battles. A fight that feels overwhelming alone can become manageable when a spirit divides the enemy's attention.

The bosses are among the game's defining achievements. Major opponents combine imaginative visual design, memorable music, elaborate arenas, and complex attack patterns. Their movements often communicate personality: some fight with disciplined precision, others with animalistic violence, and others with supernatural grandeur. Learning these encounters can initially feel intimidating, but improvement is tangible.

Margit provides an excellent early lesson. His delayed attacks punish panic, his quick follow-ups test positioning, and his aggression forces players to engage with the combat system. Defeating him feels meaningful because the battle teaches patience rather than merely checking numerical strength. It establishes that observation and adaptation will be essential throughout the journey.

Godrick is equally memorable for different reasons. His grotesque appearance embodies the game's themes of ambition, decay, and stolen power. The encounter escalates spectacularly, combining brutal axe attacks with a transformation that is both horrifying and absurdly magnificent. It is a perfect example of FromSoftware's ability to unite mechanical challenge with unforgettable imagery.

Rennala's battle demonstrates the game's theatrical range. Its dreamlike staging, magical effects, and haunting atmosphere distinguish it from conventional duels.

Meanwhile, locking is very clunky, sometimes locking something in the next room or just snapping your camera to forward which makes it even harder to regain the lock and, again, this kills you in a souls game.

Affordance is terrible.  Fans call this a feature (i.e. you don't know what level stuff is, etc.).  It would be if you could judge opponents in any way other than facetanking and dying.  You'll end up with giants you slay easily, then that small mob with a reused skin you recall from the lowbie area spanks you.  When minibosses beat you, you have no idea when you should come back.  As a result, the vast majority of what would be fun/challenging encounters are either - (a) you die, leave and maybe come back later or (b) oh yeah, let me go back there and... oh I killed it easily because I'm 20 levels higher now.

Also on a similar note, the game doesn't explain extremely important topics like leveling a weapon is more important than stats.  Or when a weapon scales with some attribute as "B" or "D", what does that even mean?

You find a boss and it barely takes damage.  Is it resistant to your damage type or are you just not high enough level?  Who knows!  Hey let's sink a ton of smithing stones into a blunt weapon just to find out and I sure hope I didn't just waste them.

Poor affordance and esoteric drops basically gating progression gives you two choices in the game: spend 10s of hours banging your head against the game to figure out the special place you need to go, to kill the miniboss, to get a drop you didn't know it had, to then give the drop to another NPC on the other side of the map, which will cause them to then sell you Smithing Stone[2] so you don't have to spend 20 hours farming Limgrave mines with a drop rate so low you aren't even sure it drops there..... OR you go to YouTube, find the cheese/needed steps and you're done in 30 minutes.

While on YouTube, you then notice some "great start to ER" videos and you watch one.  It shows you how to run around picking up all the somber smithing stones, open tons of chests and finally cheese a dragon so you have an incredibly powerful character.  All with zero real combat.  But yeah, Elden Ring is "hard" and you need to "git gud" and totally not a poorly crafted unbalanced and clunky mess of a game.

I will probably beat it in anger.  But if you don't own it, don't buy it.

Elden ring was my introduction into souls games and It did a great job of selling me on the genre.
